description: We are a curious, ambitious, and innovation-driven team united by a shared fascination with space, science, and the endless possibilities of technology. With backgrounds in artificial intelligence, software engineering, and emerging technologies, we thrive on exploring complex challenges and turning bold ideas into meaningful solutions.
summary: In 1978 astronomers found Charon, Pluto's largest moon, by noticing one tiny bump that moved from photo to photo. Charon, our app, does the same with NASA's SPHEREx space telescope, for anyone. Pick a star, search a name, type coordinates or explore a random spot, and you watch a year of real SPHEREx infrared photos of that patch as a smooth, aligned flip-book. The app then finds what moves on its own: it circles each mover, draws its path, measures its speed and direction with error bars, and checks the result against the Gaia catalog. Because SPHEREx sees a slightly different color in every photo, a year of photos also gives each mover a spectrum, which shows whether it is a cold brown dwarf. On real data it found all six fast-moving test objects (for example Epsilon Indi B: 4.35 ± 0.24 arcseconds per year, 7% from Gaia, direction within 5 degrees), with no false movers on the variable stars. SPHEREx images a billion objects and no one person can check them all; Charon turns that data into something anyone can watch and help search, including for the next Planet X.
details:
What it does

Shows any spot in the sky as a time-lapse of NASA SPHEREx photos, oldest to newest. The photos are aligned north-up, so still stars stay put and movers visibly shift.

Three ways to look: the real photos; "Changes only" (each photo minus the average sky, so still stars vanish); and "Deep view" (all photos stacked, about 3.5x less noise, so faint objects appear).

Finds moving objects automatically. It reports speed, direction, track error and confidence in plain words, for example "like a coin seen from 1.1 km away sliding its own width in a year".

Checks each find against the Gaia catalog (via SIMBAD) and shows how well they agree.

Plots each mover's brightness over time and its spectrum.

Covers all six SPHEREx detectors (0.75 to 5.0 micrometres). Cold brown dwarfs glow at the long end.

Search by star name (corrected for proper motion to 2026) or by coordinates. "Explore a random spot" sends you somewhere nobody may have looked closely.

Links can be shared and embedded: coordinates, zoom, detector and mode are all in the URL. Every photo can be downloaded as raw FITS, and every measured position can be exported as CSV.

Always current: it uses NASA's newest SPHEREx release (currently up to 5 October 2026) and shows how fresh the data is.

How it works

NASA's SPHEREx search service was down during the hackathon, so we built our own index of every SPHEREx image (about 270,000 per detector). We built it from IRSA's public copy on AWS by reading only the pointing information in each image's header. A whole-sky search takes half a second, and re-running the index picks up each new weekly release.

For a chosen spot, it uses IRSA's cutout service to cut a small square from up to 20 photos spread over the full time range. It keeps them, so the next visit is instant.

Each photo is resampled onto a common north-up grid using its own WCS. Bad pixels are filled from their neighbours using the SPHEREx quality flags.

The tracker first finds sources in every photo. It removes small pointing shifts using the stars that stay still, links sources into straight-line tracks over time, and keeps only tracks that really move, each with a fitted speed, direction and error.

Brightness comes from aperture photometry. The wavelength of each measurement comes from the SPHEREx spectral map (WCS-WAVE), and that builds the spectrum.

Validation on real SPHEREx data (20 photos over about a year)

Target Found Gaia catalog

Barnard's Star 8.7"/yr toward 351° 10.4"/yr toward 356°

Epsilon Indi B 4.35 ± 0.24"/yr toward 127° 4.68"/yr toward 122°

Kapteyn's Star 9.1"/yr toward 131° 8.6"/yr toward 131°

Groombridge 1830 5.7"/yr toward 157° 7.1"/yr toward 146°

Wolf 359 (fetched live, never cached) 5.3"/yr toward 244° 4.7"/yr toward 235°

Luhman 16 3.1"/yr toward 271° 2.8"/yr toward 277°

RW Aurigae, R Draconis (variable stars) no movers, correct about 0.02"/yr

The spectrum of Epsilon Indi B shows the water and methane dip near 1.8 to 1.95 micrometres that marks a cold brown dwarf.

Benefits

Opens a brand-new NASA mission's data to anyone, with no astronomy knowledge or software needed.

Scales the search: the computer checks every patch and people only review the circled candidates. This is the same model as the Backyard Worlds citizen-science project.

Gives trustworthy results: every find comes with error bars, a confidence level and a catalog comparison.

Tools

Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, SQLite, pyvo, and plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no build step).

Limits and next steps

Very faint movers such as WISE 0855 show up in the movie but are too faint for the tracker in single photos. Tracking on stacked photos (shift-and-stack) is the next step.

Very crowded Milky Way fields (for example Proxima Centauri) confuse the tracker.

Brightness values mix wavelengths, so they are a rough guide, not calibrated.

Next: combine all six detectors, overlay Gaia and WISE positions, and let users flag candidates for follow-up.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Select the code option, because we used Claude Code (Anthropic) to write and test code. Also select the audio option, because the demo video's voice-over is Microsoft Edge neural text-to-speech. Do not select image or video generation: all images are real SPHEREx data.
